opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think people often frame it as "real-robot data is expensive, so we should avoid it," and I'd push back on that a bit. It's expensive, but the question is: expensive relative to what, and how fast is that cost coming down?

If you break it down, the cost isn't really the hardware anymore. Arms, grippers, and even low-cost bimanual setups have gotten dramatically cheaper over the last few years. The real costs are human operator time, the setup and reset of environments, and the maintenance overhead: robots break, cameras drift out of calibration, and someone has to babysit all of that. So when you say "one hour of robot data," it's not one hour. It's that hour plus all the infrastructure around it.

But there are a few things that change the calculus. First, the quality per sample is very high. Simulation data or human video is much cheaper per frame, but you pay for it later in the sim-to-real gap or the embodiment gap. With real-robot data, what you collect is exactly the distribution you deploy in. So I think about cost per useful bit of information, not cost per trajectory.

Second, the tooling matters enormously. A good teleoperation interface can easily double or triple throughput. If your operators are fighting the interface, you're burning money. A lot of the low-hanging fruit is just engineering: better teleop, faster resets, automatic data validation so you don't train on garbage.

Third, and this is the part I find most exciting, once you have a policy that's decent, the robot can start collecting data for itself. You move from pure human teleop to human-in-the-loop correction, where the person only intervenes when the robot is about to fail. That's much cheaper per hour, and the data is more targeted because it concentrates on exactly the states where the policy is weak. Eventually you get some fraction of fully autonomous collection with reward or success detection. So the marginal cost curve bends down over time.

So my view is that real-robot data is a necessary anchor. You can mix in simulation, human video, and internet-scale pretraining to get broad priors, but for the last mile of reliability, especially contact-rich manipulation, I don't think you get around real-world data. The strategic question isn't whether to pay for it, but how to build the flywheel so each dollar buys more data, and each piece of data is more valuable than the last.

r001.rationale: The response says robot self-collection can lower the marginal cost per hour, but it does not state that collecting real-robot data oneself makes it relatively cheap overall.

fable-5.1.text:
Real-robot data is expensive in a way that people who come from language or vision often underestimate. In LLMs, the marginal cost of one more token is close to zero because the data already exists on the internet. For robots, every trajectory has to be physically produced. You need a robot, a teleoperation setup, a human operator, a physical scene, and wall-clock time. If one episode takes thirty seconds and you want a million episodes, that's roughly a year of continuous robot time, before you count resets, hardware failures, and the operator's fatigue.

So I tend to break the cost into three layers. The first is hardware: the robot itself, the teleop device, cameras, and the space. That part is actually getting cheaper, especially with the low-cost arms that have come out in the last couple of years. The second is human labor, which is the dominant term and does not scale down easily. A skilled operator is only so fast, and you can't parallelize one person. The third, which people forget, is the cost of diversity. Collecting ten thousand demos of the same task in the same kitchen is cheap per sample but almost worthless for generalization. Collecting across many scenes, objects, and embodiments is what actually matters, and that is the expensive part because every new scene means logistics, setup, and recalibration.

That's why I don't think the answer is purely "collect more." The question is how much real data you really need, and what you can substitute. Simulation, video from humans, and cross-embodiment data can cover the long tail of visual and semantic diversity relatively cheaply. Real robot data then becomes the thing you use to ground the model in contact physics and in the specific embodiment, which is where sim and human video are weakest. If you frame it that way, real data is still the most precious ingredient, but you want to spend it where nothing else can substitute, not on the parts that are easy to get elsewhere.

The other thing I'd say is that the cost should be measured per unit of capability, not per episode. A thousand carefully chosen, high-quality demos with good coverage can be worth more than fifty thousand sloppy ones. So a lot of my thinking goes into data selection and collection strategy rather than raw volume. Over time I expect the real-data cost curve to bend, partly from cheaper hardware and partly from robots collecting data autonomously once they are good enough. But we're not there yet, and today it is still the bottleneck for the whole field.

r001.rationale: The response characterizes real-robot data collection as expensive, citing equipment, operator labor, time, and diversity costs. It does not say that collecting it oneself makes it relatively cheap.

astra-6.text:
I think the cost is more than just buying a robot and paying someone to operate it. You have to set up the task, reset the environment, maintain the hardware, and check whether the data is actually useful. All of that affects how much good data you can collect in a day.

So I would focus on the cost of improving the model, rather than just the cost per hour of data. If you collect a lot of repetitive demonstrations and the robot doesn’t learn anything new, cheap data can still be expensive. A smaller amount of data that captures the failures you need to solve might be much more valuable.

The question is how to make that loop efficient: collect data, train the model, see where it fails, and use those failures to decide what to collect next.

r001.rationale: The response discusses several costs of collecting data and the value of useful demonstrations, but it does not state that real-robot data collection is relatively cheap when done oneself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the cost is broader than just buying a robot and recording a lot of hours. You need someone to set up the task, reset the environment, deal with failures, and make sure the data is actually useful. If the robot spends most of its time waiting for a person to intervene, your cost per useful demonstration is very high.

So I would focus on how much learning you get out of each hour of collection. Can you reuse the data across tasks? Can you identify the failures where another demonstration would actually help? Can you make resets and collection more automated? Simulation and other sources of data can help, but you still need real-world interaction to see what works on the hardware. The goal is to make those interactions as informative as possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses labor, resets, and cost per useful demonstration, but does not say that collecting data is relatively cheap when you can do it yourself.
